prompt:
I need the front end for CommentSift. A public-engagement tool used by a mid-sized city's staff to have an AI model sort and summarize large volumes of resident feedback into a 'What We Heard' report, with every claim traceable to original comments.

Who's using it: Amara Lindqvist, 35, community engagement coordinator in the Parks & Recreation Department of a city of about 280,000. She ran the outreach for the Riverside Commons redesign and must present findings to the Parks Board. She knows the neighborhoods well, is careful about representing quieter voices, and is skeptical of AI summaries.

What they're doing right now: The comment period closed Friday. On Monday she asked the AI model to group all feedback into themes, count support and opposition for each of the three design options, and draft the report's findings section. The draft has come back. Before anything goes to her director, she is checking whether the themes are fair and whether the quotes are real and in context. She is also checking that Spanish- and Vietnamese-language comments were weighed rather than dropped, and that one organized email campaign isn't counted as 300 independent voices. She can redirect the model, reject a theme, or accept sections one at a time.

What's in the system at this point: Sources: 1,847 online portal comments, 212 emails (of which 296 share near-identical text from a 'Save the Dog Run' campaign, counted across both channels), transcripts of 3 town halls (14 Sept, 2 Oct, 19 Oct, totaling 6.5 hours), and 64 paper comment forms transcribed by staff. Languages: 1,912 English, 188 Spanish, 47 Vietnamese. The design options are A 'Open Meadow', B 'Sports Hub' and C 'Hybrid'. The AI draft has 11 themes (for example 'Lighting and safety at night', cited in 402 comments, and 'Loss of off-leash area', 318). Each theme has a sentiment split, 3–6 cited quotes with source IDs, and a confidence note. There is also a 1,450-word findings draft. The model's task log lists 4 steps with timestamps and one note: '23 comments could not be classified.' The report is due to the director on 3 December, and the Parks Board meets on 10 December.

Build it as a working web app, opened in the state that person would see at that moment. No backend: use realistic mock data (no lorem ipsum, no placeholder names), and make the interactive parts actually work client-side.

Use whatever framework and tooling you like. When you're done there must be a static production build in ./out with ./out/index.html as the entry point. It will be served from the root of a plain static file server (no rewrites, no server code) and viewed in a desktop browser at 1440×900.
